label: SQL
description: Query-writing MCQ: filtering, joins, aggregation, NULL semantics, indexes and transactions for application developers.

questions.title: Which clause filters rows *before* grouping happens?
questions.prompt: Which clause filters rows *before* grouping happens?

options.text: `HAVING`
`WHERE`
`ORDER BY`
`DISTINCT`

questions.explanation: `WHERE` filters individual rows before aggregation; `HAVING` filters the aggregated groups afterwards.

questions.title: Why does `WHERE status = NULL` never match a row?
questions.prompt: Why does `WHERE status = NULL` never match a row?

options.text: Because `NULL` compares equal to `NULL` only in `WHERE`
Because any comparison with `NULL` yields `UNKNOWN`, and `WHERE` keeps only rows where the predicate is `TRUE` — use `IS NULL` instead
Because `NULL` is a reserved keyword that cannot appear in a predicate
Because the column must be indexed first

questions.explanation: Three-valued logic: `= NULL` evaluates to `UNKNOWN`, which is filtered out like `FALSE`. `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL` are the correct predicates.

questions.title: Which join keeps every row from the left table even when the right side has no match?
questions.prompt: Which join keeps every row from the left table even when the right side has no match?

options.text: `INNER JOIN`
`LEFT JOIN` (with the right side's columns coming back as `NULL`)
`CROSS JOIN`
`RIGHT JOIN`

questions.explanation: `LEFT JOIN` preserves all left rows; unmatched right columns become `NULL`. `INNER JOIN` drops unmatched rows and `CROSS JOIN` produces the Cartesian product.

questions.title: Why must a deterministic `ORDER BY` accompany `LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40`?
questions.prompt: Why must a deterministic `ORDER BY` accompany `LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40`?

options.text: Row order without `ORDER BY` is not guaranteed, so pages can repeat or skip rows between queries
`OFFSET` is invalid without an index
`LIMIT` only works on indexed tables
`ORDER BY` is required for the query planner to use an index scan

questions.explanation: Without a total order (ideally including a unique tie-breaker such as `id`), the database may return rows in any order, so pagination is unstable.

questions.title: Which query is valid in standard SQL?
questions.prompt: Which query is valid in standard SQL?

content.value:
-- A
SELECT customer_id, total FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id;

-- B
SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(total) > 1000;

options.text: A only — `HAVING` is a MySQL extension
B only — every selected column must be grouped or aggregated, and `HAVING` filters on aggregates
Both — `GROUP BY` allows mixing bare columns with aggregates
Neither — aggregate queries require a subquery

questions.explanation: In grouped queries each selected column must appear in `GROUP BY` or inside an aggregate, so A is invalid (bare `total`). `HAVING` is standard SQL for filtering aggregate results.

questions.title: An `INNER JOIN users` on a posts table returns fewer posts than exist. Why?
questions.prompt: An `INNER JOIN users` on a posts table returns fewer posts than exist. Why?

options.text: Posts whose `author_id` is `NULL` or points at a deleted user are dropped by the inner join
The join must be missing an `ORDER BY`
`INNER JOIN` deduplicates the result set
The users table must be empty

questions.explanation: An inner join requires a match in both tables, so orphaned posts (no author, or a deleted author) disappear. `LEFT JOIN posts -> users` keeps them with `NULL` user columns.

questions.title: Which index best serves `WHERE company_id = $1 AND created_at > $2 ORDER BY created_at DESC`?
questions.prompt: Which index best serves `WHERE company_id = $1 AND created_at > $2 ORDER BY created_at DESC`?

options.text: Two separate indexes: one on `company_id`, one on `created_at`
A composite index on `(company_id, created_at)`
An index on `(created_at, company_id)`
No index — the planner always prefers a full scan for range predicates

questions.explanation: Equality first, then range: `(company_id, created_at)` lets the engine seek to the company and scan its time range in order, which also satisfies the `ORDER BY` without a sort.

questions.title: A query needs the top spender per region. Which construct fits best?
questions.prompt: A query needs the top spender per region. Which construct fits best?

options.text: `GROUP BY region` with `MAX(total)` — it returns only the amount, not the customer
A window function such as `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY SUM(total) DESC)` filtered with a CTE
`DISTINCT ON region`, which works identically in every database
`LIMIT 1` inside a `GROUP BY`

questions.explanation: Aggregate functions collapse rows, so the winning customer disappears. Ranking with a window function inside a CTE keeps the row and ranks per partition. (`DISTINCT ON` is PostgreSQL-specific.)

questions.title: Two transactions read the same stock row, both decrement it and write it back. One update is lost. What is this, and what fixes it?
questions.prompt: Two transactions read the same stock row, both decrement it and write it back. One update is lost. What is this, and what fixes it?

options.text: A dirty read — `READ COMMITTED` fixes it

A lost update caused by read-modify-write outside a single statement; fix with an atomic `UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE id = $1 AND qty > 0`, `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, or a higher isolation level
A phantom read — only `SERIALIZABLE` in every database fixes it
Normal behaviour — last-write-wins is the defined SQL semantic

questions.explanation: Both transactions read the same value before either commits, so one write is overwritten. Making the decrement atomic in a single statement, locking the row with `FOR UPDATE`, or raising isolation prevents it.

questions.title: An import must insert new rows and update existing ones in one round trip. Which statement is the standard fit?
questions.prompt: An import must insert new rows and update existing ones in one round trip. Which statement is the standard fit?

options.text: `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (unique_key) DO UPDATE SET ...` (or the equivalent `MERGE`)
`INSERT IGNORE`, which is portable across engines
`UPDATE` followed by `INSERT` in application code without a transaction
`REPLACE INTO`, which is standard SQL

questions.explanation: Upsert via `ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE` (PostgreSQL) or `MERGE` (standard / SQL Server / Oracle) handles both paths atomically against a unique constraint. `REPLACE` and `INSERT IGNORE` are engine-specific and can delete or silently skip rows.
